📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, states Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech mentioned something about the identity of that team," indicates Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

In a recent development, israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an matter at all here," Haim mentioned, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

Recent findings suggest that "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," claims Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

Recent findings suggest that "They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

Industry observers note that when the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

Sources indicate that the first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Industry observers note that clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

Recent findings suggest that dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Sources indicate that saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.

Sources indicate that "I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

According to recent reports, saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

In a recent development, switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

Industry observers note that "To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he indicates, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

It has been revealed that "In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," notes Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

Industry observers note that "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

It has been revealed that ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," claims Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

Recent findings suggest that "It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

According to recent reports, "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she mentioned. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," states Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something upcoming, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's patch.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

It has been revealed that the upcoming rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security debuts with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.).

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA mentioned in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the firm wrote in today's enhancement.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

In a recent development, vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious concern with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's Latest Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is at the moment recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.).

NASA aims to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that releases Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Sources indicate that vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and Newly introduced Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

It has been revealed that there's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

In a recent development, the Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the organization's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 debuts on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, Latest Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 introduces (not including Sunday's failure).

Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack.

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City.

According to recent reports, manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” stated the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW.

Have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and stated: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry.

Match report: Arsenal 1-1 London City.

Tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD.

Viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an important player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji.

In a recent development, poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao.

#93942. The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2001 w)

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the latest Wembley?
  • You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
  • Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the latest Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to initiative historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler claims he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

"Then the lads wanted to do it again.".

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career.

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

Sources indicate that "There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he claims.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised.".

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other.".

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.

"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches.".

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league.".

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the major games in a way most amateur sides are not.

"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

According to recent reports, "By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand.".

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final.

In a recent development, off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

Industry observers note that they would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," claims one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now.".

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.

But even the best laid looks can go awry.

"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," notes McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley.".

According to recent reports, by hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

According to recent reports, "It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn notes. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

Sources indicate that "One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point.".

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals.

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, stated it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

"The first year was crazy, everything was brand fresh," he notes. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row.".

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

Sources indicate that the opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

Industry observers note that "In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!".

The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," claims Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year.".

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left).

Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

In a recent development, "I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening.".

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT organization after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.

"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!".

Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

It has been revealed that "Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely.".

Latest Update: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
  • Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s?
  • "Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today.".

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?".

Recent findings suggest that his straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics reveals that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

Industry observers note that the facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

Industry observers note that by 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

Sources indicate that there are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

Sources indicate that according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They at the moment own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

In a recent development, over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

Industry observers note that however, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

It has been revealed that if the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

Recent findings suggest that the deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

In a recent development, he suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices.".

But Newcastle, booed off at the break, rallied on the resumption and Martin Odegaard being dispossessed from a throw-in allowed Harvey Barnes to score while Dan Burn’s free header from a corner caused a goalmouth scramble and Malick Thiaw capitalised to poke home from a yard out.

Arsenal then lost goalkeeper Raya to injury, although they claimed a share of the spoils thanks to Madueke 12 minutes from time as the Premier League leaders moved six points clear of Brighton, who could halve the deficit when they play at Hull on Sunday.

Industry observers note that arteta said: “My feeling is we have lost two points. We were exceptional in the first half from the beginning to the end. We should have been two, three or four-nil up clearly.

Industry observers note that “When you don’t do that then the opponent is going to try to react and right from the beginning (of the second half) we weren’t at the races. One thing is to give them belief and another thing is to give them a goal. We did both.

“After that, we came back and we were exceptional. We scored the second goal and we had opportunities to go and kill the game. We lacked a moment of magic to be able to do that.

“It’s a pity because the margin should have been much bigger for the level we highlighted. I never remember that we played at that level here, never. We have won football matches playing much worse than we did today here.”.

Raya was forced off in the 70th minute, having received treatment when he slumped to the floor after coming out to collect a corner, and left the field clutching his arm with an apparent shoulder problem.

Arteta said: “Unfortunately, he had to come off, which is never good news. He will get assessed now and he will probably have an MRI tomorrow to see what it is exactly because at the moment, I don’t know.”.

Bruno Guimaraes also made way when Raya was withdrawn, with the former Newcastle midfielder’s every touch heavily barracked on his first return to Tyneside since his £75m move in the summer.

Sources indicate that arteta, though, spoke favourably of the Brazilian’s performance, adding: “It’s never easy, emotionally, you have so much going on, especially the way he feels connected to this club. But I thought he had a very good performance.”.

Matthias Jaissle reflected on a performance of two halves – but Newcastle’s head coach hopes they can take their second 45-minute display into the rest of the season.

The German said: “It was pretty clear in the first half we were not that front-foot or that intense, somehow hesitating to make the last step or last yard.

“This is something you can’t afford against a top team. But the second half was pure belief, pure conviction, no hesitation any more, pure trust between the team-mates that they are doing their jobs.

“This is the Newcastle DNA and I hope we can build on the second half.”.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.
  • Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.
  • Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” remarked marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Industry observers note that scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson noted.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage demonstrated the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench revealed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor mentioned the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson remarked, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#93934. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1782 w)

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.
  • This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
  • But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow.".

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off.

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

According to recent reports, beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In a recent development, in addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

It has been revealed that even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," states 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football.".

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

Industry observers note that they call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

Sources indicate that "I want to get away from this east-west debate," claims Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR.".

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

Industry observers note that "The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a initiative, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act.".

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition.".

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option.".

Industry observers note that support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion.".

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote unveiled two key changes:.

Suddenly, the four latest leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future.".

Industry observers note that the Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that.".

Industry observers note that for Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

According to recent reports, this season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!".

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

According to recent reports, "[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent.".

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

Recent findings suggest that "You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

According to recent reports, "It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted.".

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row.

Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
  • Recent findings suggest that most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did.
  • It has been revealed that however, newly introduced research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Recent findings suggest that most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

It has been revealed that however, newly introduced research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

In a recent development, "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Sources indicate that presently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

Industry observers note that this revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign mentioned. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

The researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

Industry observers note that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

According to recent reports, the team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

In a recent development, robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, Newly introduced Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.
  • “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic.
  • The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

“The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”.

The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

It is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data shows it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”.

Sources indicate that some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”.

According to recent reports, that 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

That is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”.

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

183 places Montenegro (16th/199th).

160 Bosnia and Herzegovina (13/173).

153 Central African Republic (49/202).

136 Cuba (46/182), Slovakia (14/150).

Pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

“The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”.

“Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

In a recent development, it is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

According to recent reports, those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

According to recent reports, “Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

The answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

Recent findings suggest that “Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

Industry observers note that “It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”.

It has been revealed that chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

Milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the new champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

In a recent development, “Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”.

“Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

Sources indicate that “Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

It has been revealed that “My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”.

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.
